food.text: The ancient Maya diet centered on four domesticated crops: maize, squash, beans and chili peppers. The first three complement one another in providing necessary nutrients, and maize was the central component of the diet and figured prominently in Maya mythology.

Much of the ancient Maya food supply grew in fields and forest gardens called pet kot. The name comes from the loose stone walls that typically surrounded the gardens, with pet meaning circular and kot meaning wall of loose stones.

Once nixtamalized, maize was ground on a metate and made into foods such as tortillas and tamales. Tortillas were cooked on a comal and used to wrap meat or beans, while tamales were corn dough with a filling, steamed in a corn husk.

Tortillas became a widespread food in Mesoamerica during the Classic period, which began in 300 BC. Because corn was sacred in Mesoamerican religions, tortillas held religious significance, and they were typically about eight fingers across and eaten with beans or chile sauce.

The Maya used slash-and-burn, or swidden, agriculture to clear land and temporarily fertilize it. The effect lasts about two years, yet the soil may stay unsuitable for planting for as many as ten years, so crop rotation was used alongside it.

Cocoa beans were used as a currency by at least 400 BC. Its social and religious significance even motivated rich hobbyist gardeners to grow it in Yucatán despite challenging conditions, though most cocoa consumed was imported, primarily from Chontalpa, Tabasco.

Archaeological evidence from the Gulf Coast of Veracruz shows that pre-Olmec peoples were preparing cacao by 1750 BC. Early Maya evidence for chocolate dates to 600 BC, when it was used in ceremonies, feasts, weddings, and as funerary offerings.
Research suggests maize may have been a staple food in the Pre-Columbian Caribbean too. Evidence of its cultivation has been found around the region, pointing to its status as an important foodstuff.

art.text: The Olmecs flourished in the Mexican states of Veracruz and Tabasco from roughly 1200 to 400 BC. The aspect of their culture most familiar today is their artwork, particularly their colossal heads. Olmec artworks are considered among the most striking of the pre-Columbian Americas.

Teotihuacan is known for some of the most architecturally significant Mesoamerican pyramids, namely the Pyramid of the Sun and the Pyramid of the Moon. They were built during a period from 1 CE to 350 CE that is notable for its monumental architecture and sculpture. Teotihuacan is also known for its vibrant, well-preserved murals.

Maya decorated pottery was made without a potter's wheel. It was delicately painted, carved into relief or incised. Chiefly during the Early Classic period, some potters used the Teotihuacan fresco technique of applying paint to a wet clay surface.

After the decline of San Lorenzo, La Venta became the most prominent Olmec center, lasting from 900 BC until its abandonment around 400 BC. Its Great Pyramid was the largest Mesoamerican structure of its time. Even after 2500 years of erosion, it rises 34 m (112 ft) above the flat landscape.

The main Preclassic sculptural style from the Maya area is that of Izapa, a large site on the Pacific coast. Its stelas, mostly without inscriptions, often show mythological subjects, some of which appear to relate to the Twin myth of the Popol Vuh. Frog-shaped altars were also found there.

Buried deep within La Venta lay opulent, labor-intensive offerings. They included 1000 tons of smooth serpentine blocks and large mosaic pavements. There were also at least 48 separate votive offerings of polished jade celts, pottery, figurines and hematite mirrors.

Around 300 CE, the Temple of the Feathered Serpent at Teotihuacan was desecrated. Construction in the city then turned toward comfortable stone housing for the population. Sometime between CE 250 and 350, political power had shifted from the temple and its palace structure to the Avenue of the Dead Complex.

Kaminaljuyú was a huge and almost completely destroyed site that once dominated the Guatemalan Highlands, and it is artistically closely related to Izapa. Among its scattered remains is Monument 10, a highlight of Late Preclassic sculpture. It is an altar with an intricate figural relief accompanied by a long inscription.

The rediscovered Olmec jade is of the quality traded throughout formative Mesoamerica, reaching areas as distant as the Valley of Mexico and Costa Rica. The richest Olmec Blue source area lies about 50 km southwest of Copán, not in the Motagua Valley as once thought.

Jade workshop areas have been documented at two Classic Maya sites in Guatemala: Cancuen and Guaytán. Archaeological investigation of these workshops has informed researchers on how jadeite was worked in ancient Mesoamerica.

Maya vase scenes and texts painted in black and red on a white underground are called Codex Style. They are the equivalents of pages from the lost folding books, and the so-called Princeton Vase is one example. Their overlap with the three extant hieroglyphic books is relatively small.

In 2010, a robot discovered a long arch-roofed passageway underneath the Pyramid of Quetzalcoatl in the ancient city of Teotihuacan. It is dated to around 200 AD. Some scholars argue that true arches were known in pre-Columbian Mesoamerica.

Stela 19 at the Olmec site of La Venta, dated to around 900 BC, is the earliest known depiction of a feathered serpent. It shows a serpent rising up behind a person probably engaged in a shamanic ritual. It shows how feathered-snake symbolism continued in Mesoamerica from the formative period onward.

war.text: Historians once pictured the Classic period as peaceful, but today it is known that both central Mexico and the Maya states were warring cultures. Their wars were never as extensive as those of the later Postclassic. War seems to be a central subject in Maya history, revealed by steles and iconography.

Teotihuacan could not have become a great political and economic center without the use of force, and its iconography attests to this. Yet its sheer power seems to have freed the city from the hostilities of other competing states.

Most ancient Mesoamerican civilizations, including the Olmec, Maya, Zapotec, Mixtec and Aztec, took human trophies during warfare. Captives taken in war were often brought to their captors' city-states, where they were ritually tortured and then sacrificed. Iconographic and archaeological evidence from across Mesoamerica documents these practices.

Despite its size, Teotihuacan is notable for lacking fortifications and military structures. At its peak around 450 CE it was the center of a powerful culture whose influence extended through much of Mesoamerica.
Monte Albán prevailed in the central valleys of Oaxaca through war, according to the steles found in Building J of the city. The Zapotec city thus recorded its military dominance in carved stone.

Around Toniná, various Maya city-states established themselves and were often hostile to each other. Steles and iconographic representations found at Toniná reveal how central war was to Maya history.

Maya battles seem to have involved many smaller raiding parties rather than large patrolling armies. Most were driven by a desire for domination and the intention to intimidate other cities. Victors often took captives back to their cities and used them for ritual sacrifice. At Bonampak, murals show a battle and its aftermath, including the torture of captives.

In some cases captives were bound or hindered so they could not fairly compete in a winner-take-all ballcourt match. The loser was beheaded, and the victor might keep his head as a trophy to confirm victory and establish his city's dominance. Maya images of trophy heads show them held by the hair or upside down, with blood or other fluids flowing from the neck, eyes or mouth.

Excavations at Teotihuacan uncovered the remains of hundreds of bodies thought to represent a mass sacrifice at the Temple of the Feathered Serpent. At the Temple of the Moon, excavators found decapitated remains and numerous bound bodies of headless males. Beneath the Feathered Serpent Pyramid, roughly 72 males, determined to be soldiers, lay in structured graves, each with 7 to 11 human jaw bones worn mostly on the arm, plus necklaces made of teeth.
Evidence from the Classic period suggests women provided supporting roles in war. They did not act as military officers, except for rare ruling queens.

Los Mangales, in the Salama Valley of Guatemala, was active from about 1000 until 400 BC. At burial site 6 there was conclusive evidence of human sacrifice: at least 12 dismembered victims and three possible trophy heads. Victims outside the crypt lay face down with wrists and ankles bound tightly together, while those inside lay face up and unbound.

literature.text: Mesoamerica, along with Mesopotamia and China, is one of three known places where writing is thought to have developed independently. Mesoamerican writing systems arose on their own, and their development represents one of very few such origins in the history of writing.

Fifteen distinct writing systems have been identified in pre-Columbian Mesoamerica, many of them known from a single inscription. Because of the limits of archaeological dating, it is hard to say which was earliest and which gave rise to the others.

In both Nahuatl and Classic Maya, one word covers both writing and drawing: tlàcuiloa in Nahuatl and tz'iib' in Classic Maya. Pictures were sometimes read phonetically, and texts meant to be read were sometimes very pictorial, so scholars struggle to tell whether an inscription records speech or is a descriptive drawing.

La Mojarra Stela 1 is a four-ton limestone slab carved in 156 CE and pulled from the Acula River near La Mojarra, Veracruz, in 1986. It carries about 535 glyphs of the Isthmian script, making it one of Mesoamerica's earliest known written records. According to Justeson and Kaufman's disputed decipherment, the text names its ruler "Harvester Mountain Lord" and tells of his ascension to kingship, warfare, an attempted usurpation, human sacrifice (perhaps of his brother-in-law), and his own bloodletting. Michael D. Coe and Stephen D. Houston, among others, dispute this reading.

The Epi-Olmec culture of Veracruz lasted from roughly 300 BCE to roughly 250 CE. With its sophisticated calendrics and writing system, it reached a level of cultural complexity unknown to the Olmecs before it. Its texts were the most detailed of their era in Mesoamerica.

In 2006, a report in Science announced the Cascajal block, a writing-tablet-sized block of serpentine bearing 62 characters unlike any seen before in Mesoamerica. Found by locals in the Olmec heartland, it was dated to approximately 900 BCE. If its authenticity and date are verified, it would be the earliest writing yet found in Mesoamerica.
The Chiapa de Corzo stela, which carries Epi-Olmec script, is the oldest monument of the Americas inscribed with its own date. The Long Count on the stela dates it to 36 BCE.

The Maya are the only Mesoamerican people known without doubt to have developed a completely phonetic script. Even so, Maya writing is largely pictorial and often shows fuzzy boundaries between images and text. The most elaborate inscriptions are considered to be those at classic sites like Palenque, Copán and Tikal.

The development of the first writing system was one of the great cultural milestones of the Middle Preclassic period, credited to either the Maya, the Olmec, or the Zapotec. Writing was part of the technical knowledge, alongside astronomy and commerce, on which social differentiation among elites was based.

Justeson and Kaufman's translation of the script on La Mojarra Stela 1 gives the ruler's name as Harvester Mountain Lord. The text tells of his rise to power, warfare, a solar eclipse, his own bloodletting, and a "dripping sacrifice", perhaps of his brother-in-law.

An Epi-Olmec stela from Chiapa de Corzo is the oldest monument of the Americas inscribed with its own date. Its Long Count date corresponds to 36 BCE. The writing system used on such monuments is very close to the Maya script, but is read only one column at a time.

The earliest inscriptions identifiably Maya have been found at San Bartolo in Guatemala and date to the 3rd century BC. An important stone block text there, from around 300 BC, is the earliest Maya hieroglyphic text uncovered so far.

Over 300 carved "Danzantes" stones have been recorded at Monte Albán, the main city of the Zapotecs by 500 BCE. The figures were once thought to be dancers, but that 19th century notion is now largely discredited. They are now seen as tortured, sacrificed war prisoners, and may depict leaders of competing centers and villages captured by Monte Albán, some identified by name.

The longest texts in the Isthmian or Epi-Olmec script are on La Mojarra Stela 1 and the Tuxtla Statuette. The script is very close to Maya script, using affixal glyphs and Long Count dates, but is read one column at a time. It has been suggested that it is the direct predecessor of Maya script, which would give Maya writing a non-Maya origin.
The earliest inscriptions in an identifiably Maya script date back to 200 to 300 BCE. Early examples include painted inscriptions in the caves of Naj Tunich and La Cobanerita in El Petén, Guatemala.

In 1993, John Justeson and Terrence Kaufman proposed a partial decipherment of the La Mojarra Stela, claiming its language belonged to the Zoquean family. Stephen D. Houston and Michael D. Coe later disputed their reading. It is still not settled whether the script is true writing or proto-writing.

In 1939, Matthew Stirling found the bottom half of Stela C at Tres Zapotes. Its Long Count date, 7.16.6.16.18, corresponds to September 3, 32 BCE. Marion Stirling argued the missing first digit was a 7, and she was proved right in 1969 when the top half of the stela was found.

The Danzante stone known as San José Mogote Monument 3 was placed as a doorstep to a ceremonial structure. Its relief shows what appears to be a dead and bloodied captive, and its glyphs depict drops of blood and a possible calendar day-name, "1 Earthquake". Such Danzantes are now seen as clearly representing tortured, sacrificed war prisoners. Dated before 500 BCE, it was once considered the earliest writing in Mesoamerica, though doubts have since been raised about whether the Zapotecs were truly the first in Mesoamerica to develop phonetic writing.

In 2006, Science magazine reported the Cascajal block, a writing-tablet-sized block of serpentine with 62 characters unlike any yet seen in Mesoamerica. Archaeologists dated it to approximately 900 BCE. If its authenticity and date are verified, it would be the earliest writing found in Mesoamerica.

During the Early Classic period, from 250 to 450 CE, writing at Monte Albán became largely limited to calendrical sequences, proper names and place names. Iconography seems to have been used for other purposes. This tendency continued and ultimately led to the abandonment of the Zapotec script.

In 2022, scholars presented evidence for the earliest known calendar notation in the Maya region: the 260-day ritual calendar date "7 Deer". It appears on mural fragments from San Bartolo that date between 300 and 200 BCE.

science.text: The Long Count calendar used by many later Mesoamerican civilizations, along with the concept of zero, may have been devised by the Olmecs. The six artifacts with the earliest Long Count dates were all found outside the immediate Maya homeland, and three of them lie within the Olmec heartland.

Mesoamerica is one of only three known places in the world where writing is thought to have developed independently, along with Mesopotamia and China. Fifteen distinct writing systems have been identified in pre-Columbian Mesoamerica, and several of the earliest date back to the 1st millennium BC.

The Classic Maya built on the shared heritage of the Olmecs to develop the most sophisticated systems of writing, astronomy, calendrical science and mathematics among urbanized Mesoamerican peoples. Their script developed between 400 and 200 BC, rooted in Olmec and Zapotec writing, and was widespread by 100 BC.
The Chiapa de Corzo stela is the oldest monument in the Americas inscribed with its own date. Its Epi-Olmec inscription carries a Long Count date that places it in 36 BCE.

Jadeite and nephrite are extremely durable, which made them highly useful for Mesoamerican technology. They were carved as ornaments, used as a medium for inscribed glyphs, or shaped into figurines and weapons. Many later jade artifacts appear cut from simple jade axes, suggesting the earliest jadeite trade served practical uses.

The Great Pyramid at La Venta was the largest Mesoamerican structure of its time. Even after 2500 years of erosion it rises 34 meters above the flat landscape. Builders also buried 1000 tons of smooth serpentine blocks deep within the site.

There is a counterargument to an Olmec origin for the Long Count. The Olmec civilization had ended by the 4th century BC, several centuries before the earliest known artifact bearing a Long Count date.

In 2006, Science magazine reported the Cascajal block, a writing-tablet-sized block of serpentine bearing 62 characters unlike any seen before in Mesoamerica. Found by locals in the Olmec heartland and dated to about 900 BCE from surrounding debris, it could be the earliest writing found in Mesoamerica if its authenticity is verified.

Artifacts from the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, including La Mojarra Stela 1 and the Tuxtla Statuette, contain calendric information in a script close to Maya writing. It uses Long Count dates but is read one column at a time. Some suggest this Isthmian script directly preceded Maya script.

The richest source of Olmec Blue jade lies about 50 kilometers southwest of Copán, rather than in the Motagua Valley as once thought. Jade of this quality was traded throughout formative Mesoamerica, reaching places as distant as the Valley of Mexico and Costa Rica.

In 2013, research at the Maya city of Ceibal used radiocarbon dating that pointed to a flux of many Mesoamerican cultures between 1150 BCE and 850 BCE. This suggests pyramid architecture spread through multidirectional influence, and that the Olmecs were less prominent in shared architectural traits than once thought.

politics.text: At its zenith, perhaps in the first half of the first millennium (1 CE to 500 CE), Teotihuacan was the largest city in the Americas. Notably absent from the city are fortifications and military structures.

When the Olmec declined, a power vacuum opened in Mexico, and Teotihuacan emerged from it. First settled in 300 BC, it had grown by AD 150 into the first true metropolis of North America and established a new economic and political order never before seen in Mexico.

In AD 378, Teotihuacan intervened decisively at Tikal and nearby cities, deposing their rulers and installing a new Teotihuacan-backed dynasty. The intervention was led by Siyaj Kʼakʼ, and the king of Tikal, Chak Tok Ichʼaak I, died on the day he arrived, which suggests a violent takeover. Tikal then became the most powerful city in the central lowlands, while its great rival Calakmul, another powerful Petén Basin city, kept up a long contest with it.

George L. Cowgill argued that Teotihuacan's most rapid growth came between about 100 BCE and 200 CE, when much of the Basin of Mexico population became concentrated in the city. At the city's height, 80 to 90 percent of the valley's total population lived there.

Cuicuilco's hegemony over the valley declined in the period 100 BCE to 1 CE, and Teotihuacan grew in importance. The decline of Cuicuilco is still a mystery, but a large part of its inhabitants resettled in Teotihuacan some years before the eruption of Xitle covered the southern town in lava. Over the next two centuries Teotihuacan consolidated its power, becoming the principal political, economic and cultural center in Central Mexico for the next seven centuries.

Teotihuacan's influence stretched across Mexico into Central America, reaching Monte Albán, Cerro de las Mesas, Matacapan, Tikal and Kaminaljuyú. Its influence over the Maya cannot be overstated, since it transformed political power, artistic depictions and the nature of economics.

During the Middle Preclassic period, Mesoamerican societies were highly stratified. Connections between centers of power let regional elites rise and control natural resources and peasant labor, and their status rested on technical knowledge such as astronomy, writing and commerce.

The Kaan kingdom was established in the 4th century at Dzibanche by the Kaanu'l dynasty. It became one of the lineages with the greatest political and military power recorded in the history of the Maya civilization.

The Olmecs were initially centered at San Lorenzo Tenochtitlán but moved to La Venta in the 10th century BC after San Lorenzo declined. San Lorenzo was all but abandoned around 900 BCE, at about the time La Venta rose to prominence. Many San Lorenzo monuments were widely destroyed around the 950s BC, which may indicate an internal uprising or, less likely, an invasion. The latest thinking is that environmental changes may have been responsible, with certain important rivers changing course.
Various districts of Teotihuacan housed people from across the city's region of influence. That influence spread south as far as Guatemala.
One of the earliest known rulers of the Kaan dynasty was Yuknoom Ch'een I of Dzibanché. His government began at the beginning of the 5th century, in the classic period of the Maya civilization.

A proposed translation of La Mojarra Stela 1, dated to roughly AD 155, tells of the ruler's ritual bloodletting by piercing his penis and his buttocks. It also describes what appears to be a ritual sacrifice of the ruler's brother-in-law. The stela comes from the Epi-Olmec culture.

In 2002 and later, archaeologists reported an Olmec ceramic cylinder seal dated roughly to 650 BCE. When rolled out, it shows logograms interpreted as "king," "3," and "Ajaw," a designation used for both a calendar date and the name of an Olmec ruler.

philosophy.text: No direct account of Olmec religious beliefs survives, unlike the Mayan Popol Vuh or the many Aztec codices. Archaeologists have to reconstruct Olmec thought from their iconography and art. They also compare it with later, better documented cultures and with modern indigenous peoples.

The Olmecs, Mesoamerica's first civilization, developed on Mexico's southern Gulf Coast before 1200 BCE. Their center of La Venta lay abandoned by roughly 400 BCE. Because scholars see echoes of Olmec supernaturals in nearly all later pre-Columbian religions, the Olmecs are often called a "mother culture".

Mesoamerican cosmology held a belief in a fundamental cosmic order in which time and space were the most important elements. Its axis mundi combined the natural and spiritual worlds, vertically made of three worlds and horizontally of four directions and a center.
Olmec religion shaped the mythological world view of Mesoamerica. Scholars see echoes of Olmec supernatural beliefs in the later religions and mythologies of nearly all pre-Columbian cultures.

The Long Count calendar identifies each day by counting the days passed since a mythical creation date. That date corresponds to August 11, 3114 BCE in the proleptic Gregorian calendar. The Long Count was widely used on monuments, most notably by the Maya.

Much of what is known about Olmec belief rests on the Continuity Hypothesis. It assumes a continuous line of religious ideas from Olmec times through later Mesoamerican cultures to the present day. Using it, researchers have discerned several separate deities or supernaturals embodying the characteristics of various animals.

Jade sculpture in Mesoamerica often depicted deities, people, shamanic transformations, animals and plants, and abstract forms. Prized for its rarity and value, jade was used by the Olmec and the Maya for symbolic and ideological ritual. Pieces ranged from single beads to large carvings.

Evidence of ritual sacrifice and the taking of human body parts as trophies exists in Maya civilization from as far back as the Middle Formative period, 800 to 500 BC. It consists of skeletal remains and Maya iconography, which commonly shows acts of human sacrifice. Captives taken in war were often brought back to their captors' cities, where they were ritually tortured and sacrificed.

No direct account of Olmec religious beliefs survives, unlike the Mayan Popol Vuh. Archaeologists reconstruct them by studying Olmec art and iconography, and by comparing them with later and modern indigenous cultures, assuming a continuity called the Continuity Hypothesis.

Early researchers believed Olmec religion centered on a jaguar god. In the 1970s Peter David Joralemon challenged this view, arguing for what are now considered 8 different supernaturals. His view has become the predominant account of the Olmec pantheon, though the field is still in its infancy.

Elite Maya wore jade pendants showing "mirror gods" associated with rulership. Mirror divination was part of Maya spiritual practice, and the sun god Kinich Ahau was often shown with a mirror on his forehead. Highly polished jade reflected like a mirror, which added to its spiritual importance.

San Lorenzo, an early Olmec center, seems to have been largely a ceremonial site, a town without city walls in the midst of a large agricultural area. Its ceremonial center and attendant buildings could have housed 5,500 people. Olmec elites there demanded symbolic luxury artifacts made from jade, obsidian, and magnetite.

Early researchers thought Olmec belief centered on a jaguar god. In the 1970s Peter David Joralemon challenged this view, proposing what are now considered 8 different supernaturals, and his view has become the predominant account of the Olmec pantheon.

Olmec religious activities were carried out by rulers, full-time priests, and shamans. Rulers seem to have been the most important religious figures, because their links to the Olmec deities or supernaturals gave legitimacy to their rule.

Los Mangales, in Guatemala's Salama Valley, was active from about 1000 until 400 BC and had elaborate burials. Its mounds held many adult male skulls interpreted as trophy heads or possibly dismembered sacrificial retainers. At burial site 6 there was conclusive evidence of human sacrifice, with at least 12 dismembered victims and three possible trophy heads lying inside the crypt. Victims outside the crypt lay face down with their wrists and ankles bound tightly together.

culture.text: At its zenith, perhaps between 1 CE and 500 CE, Teotihuacan was the largest city in the Americas. Its population was likely around 100,000, potentially making it the sixth-largest city in the world of its time. Notably absent from the city are fortifications and military structures.

The Olmecs, the first Mesoamerican civilization, developed on Mexico's southern Gulf Coast in the centuries before 1200 BCE and lasted until roughly 400 BCE, when their center of La Venta lay abandoned. No direct account of their religious beliefs survives, so archaeologists reconstruct them from art and by comparison with later cultures.

Shaft tombs in western Mexico, dating roughly from 300 BCE to 400 CE, held hollow ceramic figures, obsidian and shell jewelry, and pottery that often contained food. More unusual grave goods included conch shell trumpets covered with stucco and other appliques.

Many elements of Maya culture were shared across Mesoamerica, including two calendars, a base 20 number system, and the cultivation of corn. Human sacrifice was shared too, along with myths such as that of the fifth sun and the worship of the Feathered Serpent and the rain god, called Chaac in Yucatec Maya. Confirmation that the Maya practiced human sacrifice and ritual cannibalism came much later, for example from the murals of Bonampak.

Teotihuacan was home to complex, multi-family residential compounds, the Avenue of the Dead, and vibrant, well-preserved murals. The city covered twenty-one square kilometres, and 80 to 90 percent of the valley's population lived there. Various districts housed people from across its region of influence, which spread south as far as Guatemala.

Olmec religious activities were carried out by rulers, full-time priests, and shamans. The rulers seem to have been the most important religious figures, since their links to the Olmec deities or supernaturals gave legitimacy to their rule.

Unlike the typical Mesoamerican pyramids and rectangular central plazas, the Teuchitlán tradition is marked by central circular plazas and unique conical pyramids. This circular style is seemingly mirrored in the many circular shaft tomb tableau scenes. The tradition rose around 300 BCE and lasted until 900 CE.

The earliest inscriptions in an identifiably Maya script date to 300 to 200 BC in the Petén Basin. By about AD 250, the script had become a more formalized and consistent writing system. It was the most sophisticated and highly developed of more than a dozen systems in Mesoamerica.

The western Mexican shaft tombs were originally regarded as Purépecha, contemporary with the Aztecs, but by the middle of the 20th century they proved over a thousand years older. Nearly all artifacts came from looters, and the first major undisturbed shaft tomb was not found until 1993 at Huitzilapa, Jalisco.

At Huitzilapa, archaeologists excavated a shaft and chamber tomb with two chambers holding six dead individuals and hundreds of artifacts. Skeletal analysis showed that five of them shared similar spinal defects, so they were probably closely related, while an older woman did not share the defect and was perhaps the spouse of one of the others. Their mortuary goods included ceramic figures, jadeite, shell jewelry, conch shells, and amate paper dated to 73 CE, the oldest in Mesoamerica, found near the cranium of one of the individuals.

The site of El Arenal in the Tequila Valleys boasts a shaft and chamber tomb with a shaft depth of 16 meters. Archaeologists have found more shaft and chamber tombs in Nayarit and Colima, but none as elaborate, deep, or large as those in the Tequila Valleys of Jalisco.
